labels.reviewed: Reviewed teaching probabilities — not Qwen output
labels.illustrative: Illustrative parameter adjustment — not Qwen weights
labels.controlled: Controlled local example set — not live training

page1.title: Practise predicting the next token
page1.subtitle: Training begins with existing text and a missing next token.
page1.question: How can a model practise predicting?
page1.intro: During training, the model sees text that already exists. It tries to predict the next token, then the real next token is revealed.
page1.action: Choose the token you think came next
page1.takeaway: Training practice starts by predicting the next token in existing text. Real training chooses from a very large vocabulary.
page1.bridge: The model made a prediction. Next, compare it with the actual token.

page2.title: Compare the prediction with the answer
page2.subtitle: The target token tells the model how far its prediction was from the text.
page2.question: Was the model close to the actual token?
page2.intro: The actual token is the target. Giving it a higher probability means the prediction is closer to the training text.
page2.takeaway: A higher probability for the actual token means a smaller prediction error.
page2.technical: The technical word for the prediction error is loss. Training tries to reduce this error across many examples.
page2.bridge: The difference creates a training signal. What does that signal change?

page3.title: Adjust many numbers a tiny amount
page3.subtitle: The training signal nudges the model's adjustable numbers.
page3.question: How does the model improve its next prediction?
page3.intro: The model contains many adjustable numbers. Training changes many of them by tiny amounts so useful predictions can become more likely.
page3.takeaway: One correction makes a tiny distributed adjustment. No single number stores one word, rule or fact.
page3.technical: These adjustable numbers are called parameters or weights. Slowly changing them to reduce error is called optimisation.
page3.bridge: One adjustment is tiny. Learning needs many repeated examples.

page4.title: Repeat with many examples
page4.subtitle: Small corrections accumulate into useful prediction patterns.
page4.question: How do tiny changes become useful learning?
page4.intro: Process several reviewed groups. Related examples repeatedly nudge many parameters, strengthening patterns that help later predictions.

results.animal: The ball-related animal pattern was practised.
results.money: The savings-related meaning of bank was practised.
results.river: The river-related meaning of bank was practised.

page4.takeaway: Repeated examples can strengthen different patterns, including different uses of the same token.
page4.bridge: Repeated examples build patterns. Are those patterns the same as perfect memory?

page5.title: Patterns are not perfect memory
page5.subtitle: Useful learning applies patterns to related new text.
page5.question: Does learning mean memorising every sentence?
page5.intro: A model can sometimes memorise exact text. Its more useful ability is applying numerical patterns to related sentences it has not seen in exactly that form.
page5.correct: Correct. One repeats the same wording; the other uses a learned pattern in new wording.
page5.tryAgain: Look at whether the wording is identical or only related, then try again.
page5.takeaway: Using a learned pattern on a related new example is called generalisation.
page5.caution: If examples are narrow, noisy or unbalanced, the learned patterns can also become distorted.
page5.bridge: Put prediction, correction and repetition into one training loop.

page6.title: Follow the complete training loop
page6.subtitle: Connect training to the four earlier lessons and to generation.
page6.question: How did the model learn the patterns used to predict?
page6.intro: Training repeatedly compares predictions with real text and adjusts numerical parameters. Generation later uses those learned parameters.
page6.generationFlow: input → tokens → context → useful relationships → next-token scores → probabilities → selection → add token → repeat
page6.trainingFlow: examples → tokens → prediction → correction → adjustment → learned scoring patterns
page6.accuracy: This course shows a simplified path. Real language models contain many repeated Transformer layers and billions of numerical parameters.
page6.takeaway: Training learns the model's numerical patterns. Generation uses those learned patterns to continue text.
